Verify Now Blog > LED Sizes and Package Dimensions for PCB Design LED Sizes and Package Dimensions for PCB Design by: Mila Nov 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout LED sizes SMD LED sizes LED package sizes LED size chart LEDs are available in a wide range of package sizes, from small surface-mount devices to large chip-on-board (COB) modules. Choosing the right LED size affects more than just the component's physical dimensions. It also influences PCB layout, thermal management, optical performance, and assembly. This guide covers common LED sizes, package dimensions, and the key factors to consider when selecting LEDs for PCB design . 1. Understanding LED Package Sizes and Naming LED package sizes are generally identified by their physical dimensions or package design. However, naming conventions differ between through-hole LEDs, surface-mount LEDs, and COB LEDs. Through-Hole LED Sizes Through-hole LEDs are commonly identified by the diameter of their lens or body. Typical sizes include 3 mm, 5 mm, 8 mm, and 10 mm. For example, 3 mm and 5 mm LEDs are widely used as indicator lights. Many standard models have a lead spacing of 2.54 mm, although the actual spacing depends on the specific component. The longer lead is usually the anode (positive terminal), while the shorter lead is usually the cathode (negative terminal). However, lead length should not be used as the only way to identify polarity. Always check the datasheet or package markings before assembly. (Through-hole LED sample) SMD LED Sizes SMD LED sizes are commonly identified by four-digit codes. However, these codes do not all follow the same naming convention. For smaller indicator LEDs, codes such as 0402, 0603, 0805, and 1206 typically use the imperial system. The first two digits represent the approximate length, and the last two represent the width, in hundredths of an inch. For example: 0402: approximately 1.0 × 0.5 mm 0603: approximately 1.6 × 0.8 mm 0805: approximately 2.0 × 1.25 mm 1206: approximately 3.2 × 1.6 mm Larger LED packages used for lighting often follow metric-based naming conventions. For example, a 2835 LED measures approximately 2.8 × 3.5 mm, while a 5050 LED measures approximately 5.0 × 5.0 mm. It is important to note that an LED package code describes its approximate physical size, not necessarily its power rating, brightness, or internal chip configuration. (SMD LED sample) COB LED Sizes Unlike conventional SMD LEDs, COB (Chip-on-Board) LEDs mount multiple LED chips directly onto a substrate. They are commonly used in lighting applications that require high luminous output or a relatively uniform light-emitting surface. COB LEDs are often identified by their light-emitting surface (LES) diameter rather than by a standard four-digit package code. Common LES sizes range from several millimeters to several tens of millimeters. There is no universal naming convention for COB LED sizes. When selecting a COB LED, check its datasheet for the overall dimensions, LES diameter, mounting requirements, and electrical specifications. (COB LED sample) LED Chip Size vs. Package Size LED chip size and LED package size are not the same. The chip is the semiconductor die that generates light, while the package includes the chip and other structures, such as the substrate, encapsulation, lens, and electrical connections. A larger package does not necessarily contain a larger chip or produce more light. The actual performance depends on the LED chip, drive current, thermal conditions, optical design, and other factors. 2. Common LED Package Sizes and Specifications The following LED size chart summarizes common package dimensions for through-hole, SMD, and COB LEDs. These values are typical references rather than universal specifications. Actual dimensions and recommended PCB footprints may vary between manufacturers and models. Through-Hole LED Size Chart Through-hole LEDs are commonly used for status indicators, panel lights, and applications where the light source needs to extend above the PCB. (Through-hole LED comparison and package dimensions) Common SMD LED Sizes Note: The heights listed above are typical reference values. Actual dimensions vary by manufacturer and product model. Smaller packages such as 0402 and 0603 are commonly used as indicators in compact electronic devices. They save PCB space and are well suited to automated assembly, although hand soldering can be more difficult. Larger packages, including 2835, 3528, and 5050, are widely used in LED lighting products. The 5050 LED size is often associated with RGB lighting, but single-color and other multi-chip versions are also available. Package dimensions alone do not determine luminous flux or efficiency. When comparing LEDs, check the datasheet for luminous flux, forward voltage, operating current, power rating, and thermal characteristics. （SMD LED size comparison and package dimensions） COB LED Sizes COB LED sizes are usually described by their overall dimensions and light-emitting surface (LES) diameter. The following ranges are provided for general reference, not as a standardized classification. For high-power COB LEDs, thermal management is particularly important. Depending on the power rating and operating conditions, the design may require a thermally conductive substrate, thermal interface material, and an external heatsink. (COB LED size comparison and package dimensions） 3. How LED Package Size Affects PCB Design Selecting an LED package is not just a matter of matching its dimensions to the available PCB space. The package also affects footprint design, component placement, thermal performance, and assembly. LED PCB Footprint and Pad Design The LED PCB footprint must match the component's actual package dimensions and terminal configuration. Do not create pads based solely on the nominal package code. Instead, use the manufacturer's recommended land pattern in the datasheet. Incorrect pad dimensions or spacing can lead to poor solder joints, misalignment, or assembly defects. For through-hole LEDs, the drill diameter and hole spacing should be determined by the lead dimensions and the manufacturer's specifications. The design should also account for PCB thickness and the required mechanical fit. (LED Footprint and Pad) Component Placement and Mechanical Clearance LED placement should consider both the electrical layout and the optical and mechanical requirements of the product. Before finalizing the layout, check: Component height: Make sure the LED fits within the enclosure and does not interfere with nearby components. Optical alignment: Align the LED with light guides, lenses, or panel openings where necessary. Mechanical clearance: Leave sufficient space around the component for mounting, assembly, and maintenance. Light distribution: Consider the LED's viewing angle and position to avoid unwanted shadows or uneven illumination. These considerations are particularly important for indicator LEDs mounted near enclosure openings and for lighting boards with closely spaced LED arrays. Thermal Management LEDs convert electrical energy into light and heat. As LED power increases, heat dissipation becomes an important part of PCB design. The appropriate thermal solution depends on the LED's power consumption, thermal resistance, copper area, ambient temperature, and maximum allowable junction temperature. Common approaches include: Low-power LEDs: Standard FR-4 PCBs are generally sufficient for many indicator and low-power lighting applications. Medium-power LEDs: Larger copper areas and thermal vias can help transfer heat away from the LED. High-power LEDs: Metal-core PCBs (MCPCBs), thermally conductive substrates, or external heatsinks may be required, depending on the thermal design. A larger LED package does not automatically require a more complex cooling solution. Thermal requirements should be evaluated using the component datasheet and the actual operating conditions. For more information on heat dissipation and temperature control, refer to our guide to PCB thermal management . (LED Thermal Management) Assembly and Soldering Considerations The LED package also affects the PCB assembly process. Through-hole LEDs are suitable for manual insertion and wave soldering. SMD LEDs are generally assembled using pick-and-place machines and reflow soldering. Very small packages, such as 0402 and 0603, require more precise placement and solder paste control. Larger packages may be easier to handle during prototyping, but their pad design and soldering requirements still need to follow the manufacturer's recommendations. When designing the PCB, consider the available assembly process, pad spacing, component orientation, and accessibility for inspection or rework. 4. Comparing Common LED Packages Different LED package types serve different purposes. The right choice depends on the application's space constraints, optical requirements, power consumption, thermal design, and manufacturing process. Through-Hole LED vs. SMD LED Through-hole LEDs are useful when the light source needs to protrude from the PCB or align with a panel opening. SMD LEDs are generally a better fit for compact designs and high-volume automated assembly. 2835 vs. 3528 vs. 5050 LED Sizes The 2835, 3528, and 5050 packages are commonly used in LED lighting products. Although their dimensions are different, package size alone does not determine which one performs better. For example, 2835 LEDs are widely used in general lighting, while 5050 LEDs are often selected for RGB applications. However, the best choice depends on the specific LED model and its electrical and optical specifications. 5. How to Choose the Right LED Package Choosing the right LED package requires balancing application requirements with PCB space, thermal performance, and manufacturing constraints. Step 1: Define the Application Start by identifying the LED's intended function. Status indicators: Small through-hole or SMD LEDs, such as 3 mm, 5 mm, 0603, or 0805 packages, are common choices. General lighting: Packages such as 2835 and 3528 are widely used, depending on the required luminous output and design. RGB lighting: RGB versions of 5050 and other SMD packages can be considered. High-power lighting: COB LEDs or high-power SMD LEDs may be suitable, provided that the thermal design meets the requirements. Step 2: Check PCB Space and Mechanical Requirements Compare the LED's package dimensions with the available PCB area and enclosure space. Consider the component's length, width, height, pad dimensions, mounting position, and clearance from nearby components. For applications involving light guides or lenses, also verify optical alignment. Step 3: Evaluate Power and Thermal Requirements LED power consumption can be estimated using: P=V F × I F Where: P is the electrical power consumption. V F is the forward voltage. I F is the forward current. (For example, an LED operating at a forward voltage of 3 V and a forward current of 20 mA consumes approximately 0.06 W) This value helps estimate the thermal load, but it does not represent the actual heat generated by the LED. Check the datasheet for thermal resistance and maximum junction temperature, then evaluate whether the PCB and cooling structure can keep the device within its operating limits. Step 4: Consider the Manufacturing Process The selected package should be compatible with the intended assembly process. For example, very small SMD LEDs require accurate placement and soldering control, while through-hole LEDs need properly sized drill holes and sufficient lead spacing. For production, also consider component availability, assembly cost, and inspection requirements. 6. Mini LED vs. Micro LED (Mini LED vs Micro LED) Mini LED and Micro LED are display technologies distinguished primarily by their LED chip dimensions and application approaches. However, their size boundaries are not defined by one universally accepted standard. Mini LED is commonly used as a backlight technology in LCD displays. By using a large number of smaller LEDs, it enables more precise local dimming and improved contrast compared with conventional LED backlighting. Micro LED uses much smaller self-emissive LED pixels, with each pixel generating its own light. It is being developed for applications such as high-end displays, wearable devices, and augmented reality (AR) systems. Although both technologies use smaller LED chips, they differ in display architecture, driving methods, manufacturing processes, and application requirements. Conclusion Choosing the right LED size involves more than comparing package dimensions. PCB footprint, component placement, thermal management, optical requirements, and assembly methods all affect the final design. Always refer to the manufacturer's datasheet when selecting an LED package and creating its PCB footprint, rather than relying on package codes alone. Once the LED package and PCB layout are finalized, the next step is reliable PCB assembly. Whether your project uses small SMD indicator LEDs or larger LED lighting components, proper component placement and soldering are essential for consistent assembly quality.
